title: “The bag is cloudy, Doc”
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module text; the unit’s pediatric protocol, formulary and the attending pediatric nephrologist decide every order. No doses are given.
intro:
You are the attending pediatric nephrologist. At 10 p.m. Jenny Mendoza calls from Baliuag, Bulacan. Her daughter Kyla, 5 years old and 17 kg, has been on home CAPD (continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis) for 11 months. Tonight’s bag is cloudy, Kyla has had a tummy ache since the afternoon, and her temperature is 38.2 °C. She is drinking and talking. Yesterday the transfer-set cap fell on the floor and Jenny put it back on quickly.

The PD center is 90 minutes away and the family has no car tonight. A district hospital is 15 minutes away, with a pediatric resident on duty. Jenny asks: “Can I give paracetamol and bring her to you in the morning?”

choices.text: This is peritonitis until proven otherwise. Take her to the district hospital tonight with the cloudy bag, the home log and her PD supplies; I will call the resident now.
choices.feedback: Cloudy effluent, abdominal pain and fever already meet the diagnosis before any count. Every hour of delay lets bacteria multiply and inflames the membrane. The nearest hospital that can take a sample and give antibiotics tonight, supported by your call, is safer than a long trip or a morning visit.

choices.text: Hire a ride and bring her straight to the PD center tonight.
choices.feedback: The center has the experience, but 90 minutes plus finding transport can mean three hours before antibiotics. Treatment started nearby, with the center guiding, usually comes sooner.
choices.then: No ride can be found until midnight. You redirect them to the district hospital and call ahead.

choices.text: Give paracetamol, keep doing exchanges, and come to clinic in the morning.
choices.feedback: Fever control hides the illness without treating it. A night of untreated peritonitis raises the risk of a severe course, catheter loss and transfer to hemodialysis.
choices.then: At 2 a.m. Jenny calls again: Kyla is vomiting. They go to the district hospital.

n2.scene: The resident has never treated PD peritonitis. Kyla is alert, warm, with a tender abdomen; her blood pressure is normal for her age.
n2.prompt: What do you ask the resident to do first?

choices.text: Drain a bag and send effluent for cell count with differential, Gram stain and culture before any antibiotic; then start empirical intraperitoneal antibiotics covering gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, with doses from the ISPD pediatric table I am sending and the hospital formulary, plus antifungal prophylaxis.
choices.feedback: The sample comes first because antibiotics given before it can leave the culture negative. Intraperitoneal antibiotics reach the infection directly; the pediatric guideline sets the empirical cover, and the doses come from its tables and the formulary, not from memory. Antifungal prophylaxis lowers the risk of fungal peritonitis during the antibiotic course.

choices.text: Start intravenous antibiotics now and send the effluent afterward.
choices.feedback: Intravenous antibiotics are needed if she is septic, and starting promptly matters. But an effluent sample taken after antibiotics may grow nothing, and you lose the chance to narrow therapy safely.
choices.then: The resident has already drawn a sample from the bag Jenny brought before the first dose. You add intraperitoneal antibiotics.

choices.text: Give an oral antibiotic and send her home to continue exchanges.
choices.feedback: Oral antibiotics alone do not treat PD peritonitis reliably, and sending a febrile child home without a sample or a plan risks rapid deterioration.
choices.then: You call back within minutes, cancel the discharge, and ask for a sample and intraperitoneal antibiotics.

n3.scene: The resident calls back with the count and the Gram stain. Kyla is resting, still warm, drinking a little.
n3.prompt: How do you adjust the plan?

choices.text: Keep both gram-positive and gram-negative cover until the culture returns, admit her overnight, and transfer her to the PD center in the morning.
choices.feedback: The count confirms peritonitis. A Gram stain guides thinking but does not replace the culture; narrowing on the stain alone can miss a second organism. She is stable, so a planned morning transfer is safer than a night ride.

choices.text: Transfer her by ambulance to the PD center now, at 1 a.m.
choices.feedback: Not wrong, but she is stable on treatment, and a night transfer adds risk and a sleepless child for little gain.
choices.then: She arrives at 3 a.m., tired but stable.

choices.text: Stop the gram-negative antibiotic, since the stain shows gram-positive cocci.
choices.feedback: Gram stains miss organisms, and mixed infections occur. Narrow when the culture returns, not before.
choices.then: You restart the gram-negative cover until the culture is back.

n4.scene: The culture grew coagulase-negative staphylococcus, a skin organism. The effluent is clear and the count is falling.

choices.text: Narrow to the culture result and finish the course; watch Jenny do a full exchange and retrain the cap-drop rule; record the episode, its route and outcome in the unit’s peritonitis rate.
choices.feedback: A skin organism after a dropped cap points to touch contamination: the fix is technique, not just the antibiotic. Every episode counts toward the unit’s rate, which the ISPD sets at no more than 0.40 episodes per patient-year, and toward finding patterns across families.

choices.text: Narrow the antibiotic and send her home with a clinic follow-up.
choices.feedback: The infection is treated, but the cause is not. Without retraining, the same cap drop may cause the next episode.
choices.then: At the clinic visit you observe an exchange and retrain the cap-drop rule.

choices.text: Remove the PD catheter now to prevent a relapse.
choices.feedback: Removal is for refractory, relapsing or fungal peritonitis. Kyla is responding; removing a working catheter means hemodialysis access in a 17 kg child.
choices.then: The team keeps the catheter and completes the course.

end.title: Three weeks later
end.text: Kyla is back to nightly exchanges and school. Jenny now calls the same day when anything touches a cap, and the family has a peritonitis packet with the nearest hospital’s number, the ISPD pediatric dosing page and the center’s hotline.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Cloudy effluent is peritonitis until proven otherwise. Pain and fever do not need to wait for a count.
  • Sample first, then antibiotics, intraperitoneal, empirical cover for both gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, doses from the pediatric tables and the formulary.
  • The nearest capable hospital tonight beats the best hospital tomorrow, with you on the phone.
  • Narrow on the culture, not the Gram stain.
  • Fix the route: retrain, record the episode, and track the unit’s rate.
